card.name: Watusi
card.tagline: A 1960s American solo dance craze driven by rhythmic vertical arm movements.
card.profile: The Watusi is an American solo craze dance that gained widespread popularity in the early 1960s. Inspired in name by film depictions of Tutsi dancers from Africa, the dance became a mainstream sensation through hit pop, R&B, and Latin jazz singles. Danced almost in place with knees slightly flexed, performers alternate vertical arm movements while keeping the torso stable. The style swept television, surf culture, and pop recordings throughout the decade.
card.insight: Emerging in 1960s pop culture, the Watusi transformed vertical arm pumps and slight knee flexes into one of the era's biggest craze dances.
card.profile_long:
The Watusi emerged in the United States during the early 1960s as part of a wave of solo dance crazes that transformed American youth culture. The name of the dance derives from a historical exonym for the Tutsi people of Africa, whose traditional ceremonial dances were depicted in major Hollywood motion pictures such as the 1950 feature film King Solomon's Mines and its 1959 sequel Watusi. Although the American dance craze shared no formal choreographic lineage with traditional Tutsi performance arts, the cinematic reference provided a catchy name that record labels and vocal groups quickly adopted.

Musically, the Watusi was propelled by a succession of high-charting pop, R&B, and Latin jazz tracks. The Vibrations achieved an early R&B hit with their 1961 single 'The Watusi'. In June 1962, Philadelphia vocal quartet The Orlons brought the dance to nationwide prominence with their hit single 'The Wah-Watusi', which climbed to number two on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. The song's massive success prompted subsequent recordings and covers by major artists including Chubby Checker, Smokey Robinson and the Miracles, Annette Funicello, and The Isley Brothers. In 1963, Puerto Rican jazz percussionist Ray Barretto released his crossover hit 'El Watusi', bringing Latin jazz instrumentation and charanga rhythms into association with the trend. In Mexico, singer Julissa recorded a popular Spanish-language version of the track titled 'Mi rebeldito'.

Choreographically, the Watusi is executed as a solo dance where the performer remains largely stationary. The basic posture requires standing with knees slightly bent while maintaining alignment between the head and upper torso. From this foundation, the dancer may take one or two small rhythmic steps forward and backward. The defining movement features the arms: held almost straight with palms flat and aligned, they alternate moving up and down in a strong vertical path. Dancers may allow slight head movement to accentuate the vertical pumping of the arms. Within the 1960s American surf and beach subculture, dancers often added a stylized visual touch by simulating standing or moving in deep beach sand.

The dance quickly permeated popular media and television broadcasts during the mid-1960s. It featured prominently in television episodes of My Favorite Martian and The Addams Family, and was referenced in lighthearted dialogue in the 1967 film Guess Who's Coming to Dinner. Musical references to the Watusi persisted across decades of popular recordings, appearing in tracks by Stevie Wonder, Chris Kenner, Sam Cooke, The Beatles, The Go-Go's, Patti Smith, and Exodus. The dance also inspired derivative pop-culture variants such as the Batusi.

sections.origins_and_history: The Watusi developed in the United States as a solo craze dance during the early 1960s. Its name was drawn from a former name for the Tutsi people of Africa, likely inspired by film portrayals of Tutsi dancers in the 1950 movie King Solomon's Mines or its sequel Watusi. The trend achieved broad commercial visibility following R&B and pop song releases starting around 1961.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Watusi is danced solo with the performer standing almost stationary and knees slightly flexed. The dancer may execute one or two small rhythmic steps forward and backward. The arms are held nearly straight with flat, aligned palms, moving alternately up and down in a vertical trajectory. The head stays aligned with the upper torso but can move slightly to emphasize the arm motion. Dancers in beach and surf subcultures frequently simulated standing in sand.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance was performed to 1960s R&B, rock and roll, pop, and Latin jazz recordings. Key hit singles associated with the dance include 'The Watusi' by The Vibrations (1961), 'The Wah-Watusi' by The Orlons (1962), and Ray Barretto's Latin jazz hit 'El Watusi' (1963). Instrumentations varied from vocal R&B group arrangements to Latin percussion ensembles.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance was performed in casual party, dance hall, and beach environments. In American surf and beach culture during the 1960s, dancers performed outdoors on sand, incorporating beach aesthetic context into their movement styling.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: As a popular fad dance, the Watusi functioned primarily as recreational social dance entertainment for youth and teenagers during the early to mid-1960s.
sections.notable_figures: Key musical figures linked to the dance's popularity include vocal group The Orlons, singer Chubby Checker, Latin jazz musician Ray Barretto, and Mexican vocalist Julissa.
sections.regional_variants: In Mexico, a Spanish-language rock and roll version of 'The Wah-Watusi' titled 'Mi rebeldito' was popularized by Julissa in 1963. In American beach subculture, dancers adopted a variation simulating foot movements in sand.
sections.lineage: The Watusi is an American 1960s solo craze dance. While taking its title from film representations of traditional Tutsi dancers, it shares no direct structural lineage with African sacred or courtly dance forms. It inspired later pop culture spin-offs such as the Batusi.

basic_steps: Stand with knees slightly flexed and head aligned with upper torso.
Hold arms nearly straight with palms flat and aligned.
Alternate moving arms up and down in a vertical motion.
Optionally step forward and backward one or two small rhythmic steps.
